one_liner: Hypergraph-peeling (MWHC) minimal perfect hash builder that constructs 5-63x faster than CMPH's CHD, using ~0.5 more bits/key.
what_it_does: Builds a minimal perfect hash function over a static set of distinct keys, mapping each key to a unique integer in [0, n). The API is a C++11 class template, emphf::mphf<Hasher>, constructed from a hypergraph sorter, the key count, any iterable range and an adaptor that turns a key into a byte range; lookup(key, adaptor) returns the index, and save/load write a raw binary image. It is not a CMPH drop-in: CMPH is a C API (cmph_new/cmph_search with io adapters), and emphf's usage example is its own compute_mphf_generic.hpp / test_mphf_generic.hpp. The repo also ships command-line builders (compute_mphf_seq, _scan, _scan_mmap, _hem) that read newline-separated keys from a file.
how_it_is_fast: It uses the Majewski-Wormald-Havas-Czech (MWHC) scheme: one Jenkins 64-bit hash pass gives each key three vertices of a random 3-partite 3-hypergraph with 1.23n vertices, the graph is peeled in linear time, and 2-bit vertex values are assigned in reverse peeling order; a rank over nonzero pairs (one 64-bit count per 512 pairs) makes the result minimal, which is where 1.23 x 2 + ~0.15 = 2.61 bits/key comes from. The in-memory peeler (seq) uses the 'xor trick': each vertex stores only its degree and the XOR of the other endpoints of its edges, so adjacency is a flat array of fixed-size records, not lists. There is no per-bucket displacement search as in CHD, whose build time in the same benchmark grows from 1972 s to 23746 s as lambda goes from 4 to 6. For inputs that exceed RAM, scan_mmap implements the paper's cache-oblivious peeling (sequential scans and sorts, O(sort(n)) I/Os), and HEM splits keys into ~256-key buckets (Botelho-Pagh-Ziviani) that are each peeled in memory.
when_to_use: Static sets of 10^8-10^9+ keys where single-threaded build time matters and ~2.6 bits/key is acceptable: in PTHash's Table 5 it is the fastest-building row under 2.9 bits/key at both 100M keys (24 s) and 1B keys (374 s).
Replacing CMPH's CHD in an offline build step: 24 s vs 121-1418 s at 100M keys and 374 s vs 1972-23746 s at 1B keys, with lookups also 1.4-2.1x faster.

Key sets whose peeling working set does not fit in RAM: compute_mphf_scan_mmap builds the same structure from mmapped temporary files; the DCC 2014 paper reports 7.6 billion keys in under 21 hours on one machine.
Variable-length string or binary keys: any key type works through an adaptor that returns a byte range, hashed once per lookup.
Projects that can vendor and patch 17 small headers and do not need a maintained upstream.
when_not_to_use: Lookup-heavy paths: 199 ns/key at 1B keys (147 ns at 100M) versus 37-101 ns for PTHash configurations and 170 ns for BBHash gamma=1 in the same table; each lookup reads three random 2-bit slots plus a rank block that popcounts up to 16 words.
Space-critical uses: 2.61 bits/key versus 1.80 for RecSplit l=8,b=100 and 2.01-2.17 for CHD itself.
Multi-core machines where you want a parallel build: every construction path in the source is single-threaded.
Dynamic sets or membership tests: the structure is static, and lookup() does no check, so a key outside the build set returns an arbitrary index.

Code that needs an active upstream or portability: no commits since 2013-12-06, an open 2015 issue about an endless 'Hypergraph is not peelable' loop on a small set, an unmerged 2024 modernization PR, a Python 2 test script, and no Windows or non-x86 build as written.

integration.dependencies: none beyond the C++ standard library and POSIX (sys/mman.h, sys/time.h, mkstemp for the mmap/HEM paths); build via CMake only for the CLI tools
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (-std=c++11) with GCC or Clang; uses the GNU '?:' extension, __builtin_clzll/__builtin_ctzll and inline asm, so MSVC is out; CMakeLists declares cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 2.8), which CMake 4.0+ rejects unless CMAKE_POLICY_VERSION_MINIMUM=3.5 is set; the PTHash benchmark compiled the headers with gcc 9.2.1 in C++17 mode
integration.platforms: Unix only (CMake stops with 'Unsupported platform' otherwise); x86/x86-64 as written because bitpair_vector.hpp includes <xmmintrin.h> (unused); little-endian assumed per a XXX note in base_hash.hpp; optional SSE4.2 hardware popcount via EMPHF_USE_POPCOUNT
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Construction is single-threaded. lookup() is a non-const member (the mphf_benchmark wrapper comments 'this should be const but lookup is not const') but only reads state, so concurrent lookups on a built object look safe from the source; no guarantee is stated.

gotchas: common.hpp defines non-inline functions (logger(), nonzero_pairs()) at namespace scope in a header, so including emphf from more than one .cpp gives multiple-definition link errors; mark them inline or keep emphf in one translation unit.

Duplicate keys are not detected on the seq path and the retry loop in mphf.hpp is unbounded, so duplicates (or an input that never peels, see issue #1) retry forever; HEM restarts on duplicate hashes with the same result. Deduplicate first. The benchmphf README also reports HEM crashing with std::length_error on sets of ~1000 keys or fewer.
Build and lookup must use the same adaptor: stl_string_adaptor hashes the trailing NUL byte, so hashing (s.data(), s.size()) at lookup time returns wrong indices.

Construction logs timestamps to stderr unconditionally; seq and HEM need on the order of 30 bytes/key while building (benchmphf README); scan_mmap/HEM create 'mphf.temp.XXXXXX' files in the current working directory; save/load write raw host-endian binaries with no version or checksum.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick emphf over RecSplit (Sux) only when build time outweighs space (374 s vs 936 s at 1B keys, but 2.61 vs 1.80 bits/key at similar ~200 ns lookups), and pick PTHash instead whenever lookup speed matters (37-101 ns vs 199 ns). Its remaining niche is external-memory peeling (scan_mmap) for key sets larger than RAM; none of the sources read here compare it with SicHash, SimdRecSplit, ShockHash or ConsensusRecSplit.
verified_claims_summary: In the PTHash authors' mphf_benchmark (Table 5 of the SIGIR'21 paper), single-threaded on an Intel i9-9900K with gcc 9.2.1 -O3 -march=native, emphf's in-memory seq builder built an MPHF over 1 billion random 64-bit keys in 374 s at 2.61 bits/key with 199 ns/key average lookup, versus 1972-23746 s, 2.01-2.17 bits/key and 416-419 ns/key for CMPH's CHD at lambda 4-6. At 100 million keys the same table gives 24 s and 147 ns for emphf versus 121-1418 s and 197-204 ns for CHD; the comparison uses the benchmark authors' harness, not emphf's own.
status_note: Abandoned since 2013-12-06 (one open issue from 2015, one unmerged PR from 2024), but Apache-2.0 per the LICENSE file and only 17 headers, so it is easy to vendor and patch; last known-good compiler in the sources read is gcc 9.2.1 (C++17 mode, via mphf_benchmark).
